gist: Atwood moves from the Kabalists' doctrine of man as containing the divine prototype, through Philo, Hermes, Solomon and the Platonists on Wisdom, to her thesis that the ancient Wisdom was the fruit of an inward 'vital experiment into nature' worked by sacred arts and rites; she turns from outward physical search to self-knowledge and proposes to recover that concealed experiment.

notes.point: Kabalists give man the supreme place. Ben Jochai: the Form of man contains all in heaven and earth; no world before the human prototype. The true man differs from the apparent; that form in man, the Celestial Prototype, makes man God's image.

Divine ideas differ from imagination's idols; apparent man, 'multiplication of a blind will', differs from the Motive Reason which is his life. Man contains the total Cause of existence and, given revelation, could perceive all within himself. These writers speak from conviction.
Philo: God dwells in man's rational part as in a temple; the Logos is the seal of all things, the soul its impression.
Hermes: Wisdom is the good, fair, blessed Eternity; Mind in men is God, and some men are divine where humanity is annexed to divinity, when moved into the catholic Intuition of its Source.

Wisdom is the standard of truth in a rectified intellect; philosophy, reason's appetition for its antecedent light. Wisdom is an operative hypostasis sustaining all (the Stagyrite); Solomon: pure, all-pervading, entering holy souls to make prophets.
The outer man, senses and servile intellect dark, is left to calcine, weigh and measure matter; when that fails, extremes may meet.
Atwood looks within, asking the ancients for the method and conditions of Self-Knowledge: not trance or vision, but true, catholic psychical experience.

The Light of Alchemy requires inquiring into this experience's practical evolution. Alchemists propose reducing nature to reveal 'this Latex', destroying only the modal life, not her vehicle, and claim to have developed the Recreative Force. But they disguised the immediate efficient, the fire's direction, laboratory and vessels. Geber: men thought the confection of 'fold' (gold?) impossible, ignorant of the artificial destruction according to nature.

Causal Truth lies in a deep well: one must ascend in thought to penetrate, descending, to superstantial experience. The true light, fountain of Universal Nature, is imprisoned, cut off by the senses' outward attraction.

The philosopher: the purified soul recollects what embodiment made it forget. Plutarch: senses and passions reduce the Divine to a confused dream; freed, God leads. Rites fit the aspirant to know the Supreme Mind, whose temple is Reason, approached in sanctity of life.

Psellus: only material Rites strengthen the soul's vehicle; the soul cannot rise unaided but is led by divine illumination. Plato calls Zoroaster's magic the service of the gods. Synesius and Julian: Divine Works are needed for Divine union.

These and the Eleusian accounts confirm Wisdom was the offspring of a vital experiment into nature, arts and media bringing the central efficient into conscious being. Archytas: right investigation makes discovery easy.

The Initiated kept the means secret; ignorant of the method, we can neither test, accept nor deny the ancients. Atwood proposes recovering the ancient experiment, an entrance to the shut palaces of Mind, by descending into ourselves.

After the Hebrews, spontaneous revelation ceased; the Platonic Successor says Jupiter gave Sacred Arts instead. A soul allied to antecedent realities may feel reminiscence; its road leads to its Native Land.

method.veiled: on that form in man, which is the Celestial Prototype, rests the perfection of faith in all things
method.plain: Within man there is an archetypal form (the 'true man', distinct from the apparent man) which contains all things and is what makes man the image of God.
method.basis: II.1 ¶42: 'we must distinguish the true man from him who is here apparent' immediately precedes the Celestial Prototype clause; 'The Form of man ... contains all that is in the heaven and earth'. Identity of 'true man' with the Celestial Prototype is inferred from adjacency.

also.text: But we must distinguish the true man from him who is here apparent
no form, no world, could exist before the human prototype

method.veiled: within himself the total Cause of existence
method.plain: Because man exists, he holds within himself the whole cause of existence, and so could in principle know everything by perceiving what is in himself, if revelation were permitted.
method.basis: II.1 ¶42 states this directly.

also.text: perceive and understand all, in that all-continental All which is in himself

method.veiled: tat Motive Reason which is his life
method.plain: Man's real life is a moving, self-acting reason, contrasted with man as known here, the multiplied product of a blind will.
method.basis: II.1 ¶42 sets 'man as he is here known, the individualized multiplication of a blind will' against 'Motive Reason which is his life'.

method.veiled: God dwells, says the Jew Philo, in the rational part of man as in a palace
method.plain: The seat of the divine in man is his rational/intellectual part.
method.basis: II.1 ¶43 (Philo) and II.1 ¶50 ('this Reason is her temple wherein the Eternal Self-existent dwells').

also.text: the palace and temple of the great self-existent Deity is the intellectual portion of a man of Wisdom
For this Reason is her temple wherein the Eternal Self-existent dwells

method.veiled: the soul of man is an impression of this seal of which the prototype and original characteristic is the everlasting Logos
method.plain: The soul is stamped from the Logos, the pattern by which the world was made.
method.basis: II.1 ¶43: 'the Logos, by whom the world was framed, is the seal after the impression of which everything is made'.

method.veiled: this Mind in men is God, and, therefore, are some men said to be divine, for there humanity is annexed to divinity
method.plain: Men become divine where the Mind in them is joined to divinity, which happens when that Mind is moved into intuition of its source.
method.basis: II.1 ¶43: the clause 'when it is moved into the catholic Intuition of its Source' is attached to the statement; whether it is Hermes' or Atwood's is unclear (see ambiguities).

also.text: when it is moved into the catholic Intuition of its Source

method.veiled: namely, the standard of truth in a rectified intellect
method.plain: Wisdom, the goal of ancient science, is a corrected (rectified) intellect that serves as the measure of truth; history and observing nature's accidents cannot produce it.
method.basis: II.1 ¶44: 'Such then was Wisdom ... namely, the standard of truth in a rectified intellect'.

also.text: Intellect does not extend herself towards the intelligible Cause in vain

method.veiled: an appetition of reason for its antecedent light
method.plain: Philosophy is reason's desire for the light that precedes and grounds it.
method.basis: II.1 ¶44: 'philosophy was a desire of this kind, an appetition of reason for its antecedent light'.

method.veiled: an affirmative operative hypostasis, informing, invigorating, and sustaining all things
method.plain: Wisdom is a real, active power that forms and sustains everything, not an abstraction of the imagination.
method.basis: II.1 ¶44 states this of Wisdom 'in the ancient tradition'; Solomon's description follows.

also.text: she passeth through all things by reason of her pureness
being but one, she can do all things, and, remaining in herself, she maketh all things new
what is richer than wisdom which worketh al things?

method.veiled: in all ages entering into holy souls, she maketh them friends of God and prophets
method.plain: Wisdom enters only pure ('holy') souls and makes them prophets; nothing defiled can enter her.
method.basis: II.1 ¶44: 'therefore, can no defiled thing fall into her'; 'God loveth none but him that dwelleth with Wisdom'. Reading as a purity requirement on the operator is inferred.

also.text: therefore, can no defiled thing fall into her

method.veiled: with his senses and servile intellect all dark within
method.plain: The outer, sense-bound man and his outward experiments (calcining, weighing, measuring matter) cannot reach the secret; Atwood sets that route aside.
method.basis: II.1 ¶45 leaves the outer man 'to work with his own instruments'; II.1 ¶46 says many 'foundered' seeking in the outer world.

also.text: there to calcine, weight, and measure circumferences, from the first to the last round of material possibility
seek not at random any longer in the outer world where so many before have foundered

method.veiled: we look within
method.plain: The search is directed inward, toward self-knowledge, guided by the ancients' instructions on its method and conditions.
method.basis: II.1 ¶46: 'inquire of the wise ancients to direct us about the true method and conditions of Self-Knowledge'; II.1 ¶53 'Let us descend into ourselves'.

also.text: Let us descend into ourselves, and believe in ourselves if we be able, that that which we are is worthy of our investigation

method.veiled: the true psychical experience, catholic
method.plain: What is investigated is a real, universal psychical experience, explicitly not ordinary trance, day-dream or fanatical vision.
method.basis: II.1 ¶46: 'no common trance or day-dream, or any fanatical vision of celestials, that we propose to scrutinize, but the true psychical experience'.

method.veiled: such a reducation of nature as shall discover this Latex without destroying her vehicle, but the modal life only
method.plain: The work reduces nature so as to expose a hidden principle, destroying only its present mode of life and not the bearer that carries it, i.e. casting off nature's superfluous forms.
method.basis: II.1 ¶47 also speaks of 'the rejection of her superfluous forms'. 'Latex' and 'vehicle' are not explained in this chunk (see ambiguities).

also.text: where nature may be addressed in order to the rejection of her superfluous forms

method.veiled: man, by rationally conditionating, has succeeded in developing into action the Recreative Force
method.plain: The alchemists claim that man, by setting up the right conditions rationally, has brought a re-creating power into action.
method.basis: II.1 ¶47 reports the alchemists' profession; the nature of the Recreative Force is not further explained here.

method.veiled: what was their immediate efficient? Whence and whereon did they direct their fire?
method.plain: The concealed points of the method: the direct active cause, the source and target of the 'fire', and what the laboratory and vessels stand for. Atwood says these were deliberately disguised; this chunk does not decode them.
method.basis: II.1 ¶47: 'These things, with the laboratory, its vessels and various apparatus, they have disguised'.

also.text: These things, with the laboratory, its vessels and various apparatus, they have disguised

method.veiled: the artificial destruction according to the course of nature
method.plain: A deliberate dissolution performed in accordance with nature is required for the confection (of 'fold', apparently gold); ignorance of it led men to think the work impossible. Not explained further here.
method.basis: II.1 ¶47 (Geber): men thought the confection impossible 'because they have not know' this destruction; connects with the 'reducation of nature' in the same paragraph.

also.text: they have proved it to be of a strong composition, but of how strong a composition they have not proven

method.veiled: he must ascend in thought who would, descending, hope to penetrate so far as to the superstantial experience of things
method.plain: To reach the deepest (causal) experience one must first rise in thought; a shallow reason cannot sound it.
method.basis: II.1 ¶49: 'The well out of which she is drawn is deep, and not therefore to be fathomed by the plummet of a shallow reason'.

also.text: The well out of which she is drawn is deep, and not therefore to be fathomed by the plummet of a shallow reason

method.veiled: the true light shut up as in a prison, the fountain of Universal Nature separated off from human understanding by the external attraction of it through the gates of sense
method.plain: The source-light of nature is present but cut off from our understanding because our attention is drawn outward through the senses.
method.basis: II.1 ¶49 states the cause of the separation directly.

method.veiled: becoming purified from the body, will recollect all those things, the remembrance of which she loses in the present life
method.plain: Purification from bodily involvement restores the soul's self-contemplation and memory of what it has forgotten.
method.basis: II.1 ¶50: in the body 'she departs from self-contemplation'; purified, she recollects.

also.text: whether it be possible to approach to a recollection of this ancient experiment

method.veiled: encompassed about with senses and passions
method.plain: Senses and passions limit the soul's share in the Divine to dim glimpses; once freed from them, God becomes the soul's guide.
method.basis: II.1 ¶50 (Plutarch): 'obscure glimmerings ... a confused dream'; 'when they are freed from these impediments ... it is then that God becomes our leader'.

also.text: any further than by obscure glimmerings, and as it were, in comparison, a confused dream
it is then that God becomes our leader

method.veiled: the end of which, as of all ceremonial rites and disciplines, was that the aspirant might be prepared and fitted for the attainment of the knowledge of the Supreme Mind
method.plain: The aspirant must be prepared by holiness, rites and discipline; the Supreme Mind is approached only with solemnity and sanctity of life. Desire for Truth is itself aspiration to the Divine Nature.
method.basis: II.1 ¶50: 'to desire and covet after the Truth is to aspire to be a partaker of the Divine Nature itself'; 'but with due solemnity, and sanctity of life'.

also.text: but with due solemnity, and sanctity of life

method.veiled: there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites
method.plain: The soul (its 'vehicle') is strengthened and perfected only through material rites, i.e. through the power of materials on earth, which Plato calls the service of the gods.
method.basis: II.1 ¶51: 'To initiate or perfect the human soul by the power of materials here on earth'. What the rites and materials are is not specified (see ambiguities).

also.text: To initiate or perfect the human soul by the power of materials here on earth
calls the magic of Zoroaster the service of the gods

method.veiled: the work of Piety leads it by the hand of God, by illumination from thence
method.plain: The soul's highest faculty cannot rise to the Divine by itself; it is led by divine illumination through the work of piety, and (Synesius, Julian) without such Divine Works the union is neither achieved nor understood.
method.basis: II.1 ¶51: 'the supreme faculty of the soul cannot by its own guidance aspire'; II.1 ¶52 Julian: 'without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood'.

also.text: without such assistance the Divine union is neither effected not rightly understood
bears witness to the efficacy of Divine Works

method.veiled: Wisdom was the offspring of a vital experiment into nature, by certain arts and media producing the central efficient into conscious being and effect
method.plain: Atwood's thesis: ancient Wisdom resulted from a living experiment on nature, using specific arts and means to bring the central active cause into conscious existence and operation.
method.basis: II.1 ¶52, presented as confirmed by the Eleusian accounts and the philosophers cited.

method.veiled: has given us observation through Sacred Arts, by which we have at hand sufficient assistance
method.plain: Since spontaneous revelation ceased, communion with the divine is reached by experimental research through sacred arts.
method.basis: II.1 ¶53: spontaneous revelation 'without experimental research' ceased after the Hebrews; Sacred Arts given 'that we might not be deprived of all communication with the gods'.

method.veiled: being ignorant of the method, how should we presume to test the truth of this philosophy?
method.plain: The Initiated kept the means secret, so the claims cannot be tested without recovering the method; right investigation is the key.
method.basis: II.1 ¶53: 'the Initiated were so profoundly silent upon these means'; II.1 ¶52 Archytas on investigating rightly.

also.text: If you investigate rightly, says Archytas, discovery will be easy for you
that the Initiated were so profoundly silent upon these means

method.veiled: should find familiar scenes recur, thrilling into reminiscence, as of some long past life forgotten
method.plain: A sign of aptitude: a soul more allied to antecedent realities feels the material as a recollection of something forgotten; such a one is on the road 'towards his Native Land'.
method.basis: II.1 ¶53: 'a less oblivious soul or intellect, more allied than ordinary to antecedent realities'.

also.text: the road whereon we are journeying is towards his Native Land

method.veiled: whether there be still an entrance open, as there was once said to be, to the shut palaces of Mind
method.plain: The goal is access to the mind's hidden interior; Wisdom so reached would be a real, attainable good, not an outward acquisition.
method.basis: II.1 ¶53: 'the Wisdom of the ancients was not the outward, adventitious acquisition ... but a very real, substantial, and attainable good'; image of the palace as seat of God in II.1 ¶43.

also.text: a very real, substantial, and attainable good

ambiguities.quote: when it is moved into the catholic Intuition of its Source
readings: Atwood's own qualifying addition to Hermes.
ambiguities.basis: The footnote marker (41) falls just before this clause, suggesting the citation ends there and the clause is Atwood's; but it continues the same sentence.

ambiguities.quote: such a reducation of nature as shall discover this Latex without destroying her vehicle
readings: 'this Latex' refers back to 'the true Light of Alchemy' in the preceding clause.
'this Latex' is a hidden (latent) principle in nature, linked to the 'Recreative Force' named next.
ambiguities.basis: 'this' implies an antecedent; 'the true Light of Alchemy' precedes in the same sentence; 'Recreative Force' follows in the next clause.

readings: 'sold' is a misprint for 'soul' (the vehicle of the soul).
The 'vehicle' here is the same as nature's 'vehicle' preserved in II.1 ¶47.
ambiguities.basis: The following sentence speaks of perfecting 'the human soul'; ¶47 uses 'her vehicle' of nature; the text does not connect them.

ambiguities.quote: And all this because they knew not the verity Of altitude, latitude, and of profundity
readings: Refers to Geber's 'how strong a composition' — the full extent of the matter's composition.
Anticipates the depth image of II.1 ¶49 (the deep well; ascending and descending).
ambiguities.basis: Follows Geber directly in ¶47; ¶49 develops depth and ascent/descent. The verse is not explained.

ambiguities.quote: there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites
readings: Literal ceremonial rites using physical materials.
The material arts Atwood equates with the 'vital experiment into nature' (II.1 ¶52).
ambiguities.basis: ¶51 speaks of 'the power of materials here on earth'; ¶52 says Wisdom came 'by certain arts and media'.

threads.note: 'the Stagyrite before cited' — an earlier citation of the Stagyrite.
'nor is this the only place in Scripture where we have a promise with Wisdom' — other scriptural passages, unspecified.
'as we have seen' — the alchemists' proposed reduction of nature was discussed earlier.
'as we have already shown' — earlier demonstration that the alchemists disguised their fire, laboratory, vessels and apparatus.
'as we before said' — earlier remark that this research may seem appalling or nugatory to readers.
'Here, then, we take up our clue to weave onward as we proceed, unraveling the Mysteries by their traditional light' — announces the coming treatment of the Mysteries and the ancient experiment.
